lead: A microstrip patch antenna is a thin metal patch printed on a grounded dielectric sheet. The patch and ground form a resonant cavity; the electric field fringes at the patch edges and those fringing fields radiate. It is cheap, flat and easy to etch onto a circuit board, so it sits inside phones, Wi-Fi routers, GPS receivers and radar panels. Its price is narrow bandwidth and modest gain. This chapter shows why the patch resonates, how to size a rectangular patch, and how feeds and arrays make it useful.
prereq: You need: microstrip line behaviour from Unit 1 and antenna parameters from Unit 2; array ideas appear later in chapter 3.1.

sections.h3: The patch as a resonant radiator

blocks.text: A rectangular patch of length L and width W is etched on a substrate of thickness h and relative permittivity ε<sub>r</sub>. A continuous copper ground plane sits under the substrate. The patch is a resonator, not a travelling-wave line: at resonance the voltage is maximum at the two edges separated by L and near zero at the centre. The field between patch and ground is mostly inside the dielectric, but some field spills past the edges.

This fringing field has a vertical component at the edges. The two edges perpendicular to L therefore act like narrow radiating slots. The other pair of edges radiates weakly and mostly in unwanted directions. A patch is low profile, light and can be made by PCB etching. It is used in Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, GPS, mobile handsets and phased-array radar. Substrate choice controls size and bandwidth: higher ε<sub>r</sub> shrinks the patch; thicker, lower-ε<sub>r</sub> foam gives more bandwidth but can launch surface waves.

Treat the patch as a microstrip transmission line of width W and length L, open-circuited at both ends. The open ends are not perfect magnetic walls: the field fringes by a length ΔL beyond each edge. The electrical length is therefore L + 2ΔL, and resonance occurs when this length is half a wavelength in the effective medium. The effective permittivity ε<sub>eff</sub> accounts for fields in both dielectric and air. First pick W for good radiation and reasonable impedance.

blocks.where: W is patch width in metres; c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s; f is resonant frequency in Hz; ε<sub>r</sub> is substrate relative permittivity.
ε<sub>eff</sub> is effective relative permittivity; h is substrate thickness in metres; W is patch width in metres.
ΔL is the fringing extension at one open edge in metres; ε<sub>eff</sub> is from the previous formula.
L is patch length in metres; the first term is half a guided wavelength; 2ΔL corrects both open ends.

blocks.text: The dominant mode is TM<sub>10</sub>. The fringing length makes L slightly shorter than half the guided wavelength. The resonant frequency is f = c/(2(L+2ΔL)√ε<sub>eff</sub>).

Three feeds are common. An inset feed cuts a microstrip line into the patch; the inset depth sets the input resistance. A probe feed comes up through the ground and substrate from a coaxial line; it works well on thick substrates. An aperture feed couples through a slot in the ground from a line below; it reduces spurious radiation from the feed line. The patch itself is a thin resonator, so its impedance bandwidth is only a few percent. Thicker substrate, lower ε<sub>r</sub>, parasitic patches and slots can widen it.

A single patch has modest gain, often about 5–8 dBi. A patch array multiplies the element pattern by an array factor, as in chapter 3.1; spacing and phase follow the uniform and tapered arrays of chapter 3.2 and chapter 3.3. Feed networks and MMIC integration belong to Unit 4. Some syllabi add fractal patches or millimetre-wave patches for 5G; only a few universities examine fractal design in detail.

examples.question: Design a rectangular microstrip patch to resonate at f = 2.4 GHz on a substrate with ε<sub>r</sub> = 4.4 and h = 1.6 mm. Use the transmission-line model with c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Find W, ε<sub>eff</sub>, the fringing extension ΔL and L. State the dominant mode.
steps: Compute the free-space length factor: c/(2f) = (3.0 × 10⁸)/(2 × 2.4 × 10⁹) = 0.0625 m.
The dominant mode is TM<sub>10</sub>, with radiation mainly from the two edges separated by L.
examples.answer: The patch is W ≈ 38.036 mm and L ≈ 29.441 mm, with ε<sub>eff</sub> ≈ 4.086 and ΔL ≈ 0.739 mm, operating in the TM<sub>10</sub> mode.

traps: Do not use λ₀/2 for the patch length. The dielectric slows the wave, so use ε<sub>eff</sub> and subtract the fringing length 2ΔL.
Do not substitute ε<sub>eff</sub> into the width formula. W uses the substrate ε<sub>r</sub>; ε<sub>eff</sub> is used for the guided wavelength and ΔL.
The patch edge is not a 50 Ω point. The input resistance changes with inset depth or probe position; a direct edge feed is often a few hundred ohms.
The patch is narrowband, not wideband. A thicker substrate or lower ε<sub>r</sub> helps, but it also increases surface waves and unwanted radiation.

quiz.q: Name the three main layers of a microstrip patch and give one function of each.
quiz.a: Patch: resonates and radiates from its edges. Substrate: supports the field and sets electrical size. Ground: completes the cavity and reflects fields.

quiz.q: Why is the physical patch length slightly less than half the guided wavelength?
quiz.a: The open ends fringe by ΔL at each edge, so L + 2ΔL equals half a guided wavelength. Hence L is shorter than that half wavelength by 2ΔL.

quiz.q: Find W for a patch at f = 5 GHz on ε<sub>r</sub> = 2.2 with c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Use the width formula.
A designer doubles the substrate height while keeping the same patch. State two effects and one design correction.
quiz.a: Bandwidth usually increases because Q falls. Fringing grows, so ε<sub>eff</sub> and ΔL change and the resonant frequency shifts. Correction: retune L, and check surface-wave and cross-polarisation loss.

quiz.q: Why does ε<sub>eff</sub> lie between 1 and ε<sub>r</sub>?
quiz.a: Part of the field is in air and part is in the dielectric. ε<sub>eff</sub> is a weighted average of 1 and ε<sub>r</sub>, so it lies between them.

quiz.q: A patch resonates at 2.4 GHz. If ε<sub>r</sub> is increased and L is unchanged, what happens to the resonant frequency? How can it be restored?
quiz.a: f ∝ 1/√ε<sub>eff</sub>, so the resonant frequency falls. Restore it by shortening L, and recompute W and ΔL for the new substrate.

quiz.q: Compare inset and probe feeds for a 3 mm thick foam substrate.
quiz.a: A probe feed is better for a thick substrate: it feeds directly through the ground, has low spurious radiation and does not need a wide inset. An inset feed is simple on thin PCB material, but at 3 mm it needs a large inset and the feed line can radiate.

beyond: Not for the exam. Patch antennas now appear in millimetre-wave 5G arrays, where many small patches are spaced about half a wavelength and fed by a corporate network. Fractal and parasitic patch shapes are studied for multiband behaviour, but their design is iterative and simulation-heavy. Wearable and textile patches use conductive fabric on felt or foam. Search next for cavity model of a patch, inset feed design, defected ground structures for bandwidth, and patch arrays for beam steering.
